# futures-lite 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-lite/^2

# futures-lite

A lightweight async prelude.

This crate is a subset of [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) that compiles an order of magnitude faster, fixes minor
warts in its API, fills in some obvious gaps, and removes almost all unsafe code from it.

In short, this crate aims to be more enjoyable than [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) but still fully compatible with
it.

The API for this crate is intentionally constrained. Please consult the
[features list](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite/blob/master/FEATURES.md) for APIs that are occluded from this crate.

## Examples

```
use future;
```

# wasm-bindgen-futures 0.4.75 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-futures/0.4.75

`wasm-bindgen-futures`

This crate bridges the gap between Rust `Future`s and JavaScript `Promise`s.

As of this version the implementation lives in [ js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys) under the

`futures`
feature. Depending on this crate automatically activates that feature, which
gives `js_sys::Promise` a first-class `IntoFuture` implementation — meaning
you can `.await` any `Promise` directly:```
use Promise;
use *;
async
```
All public items from the previous API are re-exported unchanged for backwards compatibility:

- `JsFuture`- `Promise`into a named- `Future`type
- `spawn_local`- `Future<Output = ()>`on the JS microtask queue
- `future_to_promise`- `Future`into a JS- `Promise`
- `future_to_promise_typed`- `future_to_promise`

Under the feature flag `futures-core-03-stream` there is support for
`AsyncIterator` to `Stream` conversion via `JsStream`.

See the [API documentation](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/api/wasm_bindgen_futures/) for more info.

---

# wasm-bindgen-futures 0.4.53 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-futures/0.4.53

`wasm-bindgen-futures`

This crate bridges the gap between a Rust `Future` and a JavaScript
`Promise`. It provides two conversions:

- From a JavaScript `Promise`into a Rust`Future`.
- From a Rust `Future`into a JavaScript`Promise`.

Additionally under the feature flag `futures-core-03-stream` there is experimental
support for `AsyncIterator` to `Stream` conversion.

See the [API documentation](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/api/wasm_bindgen_futures/) for more info.

---

# wasm-bindgen-futures 0.4.52 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-futures/0.4.52

`wasm-bindgen-futures`

This crate bridges the gap between a Rust `Future` and a JavaScript
`Promise`. It provides two conversions:

- From a JavaScript `Promise`into a Rust`Future`.
- From a Rust `Future`into a JavaScript`Promise`.

Additionally under the feature flag `futures-core-03-stream` there is experimental
support for `AsyncIterator` to `Stream` conversion.

See the [API documentation](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/api/wasm_bindgen_futures/) for more info.

# js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys

## Expand description

Bindings to JavaScript’s standard, built-in objects, including their methods and properties.

This does *not* include any Web, Node, or any other JS environment
APIs. Only the things that are guaranteed to exist in the global scope by
the ECMAScript standard.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-about-camelcase-snake_case-and-naming-conventions)A Note About `camelCase`, `snake_case`, and Naming Conventions

JavaScript’s global objects use `camelCase` naming conventions for functions
and methods, but Rust style is to use `snake_case`. These bindings expose
the Rust style `snake_case` name. Additionally, acronyms within a method
name are all lower case, where as in JavaScript they are all upper case. For
example, `decodeURI` in JavaScript is exposed as `decode_uri` in these
bindings.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-about-tostring-and-to_js_string)A Note About `toString` and `to_js_string`

JavaScript’s `toString()` method is exposed as `to_js_string()` in these
bindings to avoid confusion with Rust’s [ ToString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html) trait and its

`to_string()` method. This allows types to implement both the Rust
[trait (which provides](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display``to_string()` via
[) and still expose the JavaScript](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html)

`ToString``toString()` functionality.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wasm_bindgen](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [Atomics](https://docs.rs/Atomics/index.html)
- The `Atomics`object provides atomic operations as static methods. They are used with`SharedArrayBuffer`objects.
- [Intl](https://docs.rs/Intl/index.html)
- [JSON](https://docs.rs/JSON/index.html)
- The `JSON`object contains methods for parsing[JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)](https://json.org/)and converting values to JSON. It can’t be called or constructed, and aside from its two method properties, it has no interesting functionality of its own.
- [Math](https://docs.rs/Math/index.html)
- [Reflect](https://docs.rs/Reflect/index.html)
- [WebAssembly](https://docs.rs/WebAssembly/index.html)

- Bridging between JavaScript `Promise`s and Rust`Future`s.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_uri.html)- uri
- The `decodeURI()`function decodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) previously created by`encodeURI`or by a similar routine.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_uri_component.html)- uri_ - component
- The `decodeURIComponent()`function decodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) component previously created by`encodeURIComponent`or by a similar routine.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_uri.html)- uri
- The `encodeURI()`function encodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) by replacing each instance of certain characters by one, two, three, or four escape sequences representing the UTF-8 encoding of the character (will only be four escape sequences for characters composed of two “surrogate” characters).
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_uri_component.html)- uri_ - component
- The `encodeURIComponent()`function encodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) component by replacing each instance of certain characters by one, two, three, or four escape sequences representing the UTF-8 encoding of the character (will only be four escape sequences for characters composed of two “surrogate” characters).
- [escape](https://docs.rs/fn.escape.html)
- The `escape()`function computes a new string in which certain characters have been replaced by a hexadecimal escape sequence.
- [eval](https://docs.rs/fn.eval.html)
- The `eval()`function evaluates JavaScript code represented as a string.
- [global](https://docs.rs/fn.global.html)
- Returns a handle to the global scope object.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_finite.html)- finite
- The global `isFinite()`function determines whether the passed value is a finite number. If needed, the parameter is first converted to a number.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_float.html)- float
- The `parseFloat()`function parses an argument and returns a floating point number, or NaN on error.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_int.html)- int
- The `parseInt()`function parses a string argument and returns an integer of the specified radix (the base in mathematical numeral systems), or NaN on error.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_iter.html)- iter
- Create an iterator over `val`using the JS iteration protocol and`Symbol.iterator`.
- [unescape](https://docs.rs/fn.unescape.html)
- The `unescape()`function computes a new string in which hexadecimal escape sequences are replaced with the character that it represents. The escape sequences might be introduced by a function like`escape`. Usually,`decodeURI`or`decodeURIComponent`are preferred over`unescape`.

# spawn_local in js_sys::futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/*/js_sys/futures/fn.spawn_local.html

`pub fn spawn_local<F>(future: F)`## Expand description

Runs a Rust `Future` on the current thread.

The `future` must be `'static` because it will be scheduled
to run in the background and cannot contain any stack references.

The `future` will always be run on the next microtask tick even if it
immediately returns `Poll::Ready`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This function has the same panic behavior as `future_to_promise`.

---

# future_to_promise in js_sys::futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/*/js_sys/futures/fn.future_to_promise.html

`pub fn future_to_promise<F>(future: F) -> `[Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)## Expand description

Converts a Rust `Future` into a JavaScript `Promise`.

This function will take any future in Rust and schedule it to be executed,
returning a JavaScript `Promise` which can then be passed to JavaScript.

The `future` must be `'static` because it will be scheduled to run in the
background and cannot contain any stack references.

The returned `Promise` will be resolved or rejected when the future
completes, depending on whether it finishes with `Ok` or `Err`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Note that in Wasm panics are currently translated to aborts, but “abort” in this case means that a JavaScript exception is thrown. The Wasm module is still usable (likely erroneously) after Rust panics.

---

# future_to_promise_typed in js_sys::futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/*/js_sys/futures/fn.future_to_promise_typed.html

```
pub fn future_to_promise_typed<T, F>(
    future: F,
) ->
```
[Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<<T as [Promising](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html)>::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>## Expand description

Converts a Rust `Future` into a corresponding typed JavaScript `Promise<T>`.

This function will take any future in Rust and schedule it to be executed,
returning a JavaScript `Promise` which can then be passed to JavaScript.

The `future` must be `'static` because it will be scheduled to run in the
background and cannot contain any stack references.

The returned `Promise` will be resolved or rejected when the future completes,
depending on whether it finishes with `Ok` or `Err`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Note that in Wasm panics are currently translated to aborts, but “abort” in this case means that a JavaScript exception is thrown. The Wasm module is still usable (likely erroneously) after Rust panics.

If the `future` provided panics then the returned `Promise` **will not
resolve**. Instead it will be a leaked promise. This is an unfortunate
limitation of Wasm currently that’s hoped to be fixed one day!

# wasm-bindgen-futures 0.4.76 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-futures/latest/source/README.md

```
[API Documentation][docs]
This crate bridges the gap between Rust `Future`s and JavaScript `Promise`s.
As of this version the implementation lives in [`js-sys`] under the `futures`
feature. Depending on this crate automatically activates that feature, which
gives `js_sys::Promise` a first-class `IntoFuture` implementation — meaning
you can `.await` any `Promise` directly:
```rust
use js_sys::Promise;
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
async fn example(promise: Promise) -> Result<JsValue, JsValue> {
}
```
All public items from the previous API are re-exported unchanged for backwards
compatibility:
- ---
Under the feature flag `futures-core-03-stream` there is support for
`AsyncIterator` to `Stream` conversion via `JsStream`.
See the [API documentation][docs] for more info.
```

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/js-sys/0.3.103

Bindings for all JS global objects and functions in all JS environments like
Node.js and browsers, built on `#[wasm_bindgen]` using the `wasm-bindgen` crate.

Raw bindings to JS global APIs for projects using wasm-bindgen. This crate is
handwritten and intended to work in all JS environments like browsers and
Node.js.

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

---

# futures_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-util/^0.3.31/

## Expand description

Combinators and utilities for working with `Future`s, `Stream`s, `Sink`s,
and the `AsyncRead` and `AsyncWrite` traits.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::future::`- [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html);
- `pub use crate::future::`- [FutureExt](https://docs.rs/future/trait.FutureExt.html);
- `pub use crate::future::`- [TryFuture](https://docs.rs/future/trait.TryFuture.html);
- `pub use crate::future::`- [TryFutureExt](https://docs.rs/future/trait.TryFutureExt.html);
- `pub use crate::stream::`- [Stream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.Stream.html);
- `pub use crate::stream::`- [StreamExt](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.StreamExt.html);
- `pub use crate::stream::`- [TryStream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.TryStream.html);
- `pub use crate::stream::`- [TryStreamExt](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.TryStreamExt.html);
- `pub use crate::sink::`- [Sink](https://docs.rs/sink/trait.Sink.html);- `sink`
- `pub use crate::sink::`- [SinkExt](https://docs.rs/sink/trait.SinkExt.html);- `sink`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncBufRead](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncBufRead.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncBufReadExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncBufReadExt.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncRead](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncRead.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncReadExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncReadExt.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncSeek](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncSeek.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncSeekExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncSeekExt.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncWrite](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html);- `io`and- `std`
- `pub use crate::io::`- [AsyncWriteExt](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncWriteExt.html);- `io`and- `std`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [compat](https://docs.rs/compat/index.html)- `compat`
- Interop between `futures`0.1 and 0.3.
- [future](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)
- Asynchronous values.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)- `io`
- Asynchronous I/O.
- [lock](https://docs.rs/lock/index.html)- `alloc`
- Futures-powered synchronization primitives.
- [never](https://docs.rs/never/index.html)
- This module contains the `Never`type.
- [sink](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)- `sink`
- Asynchronous sinks.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- Asynchronous streams.
- [task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)
- Tools for working with tasks.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await-macro`and- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await-macro`and- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await-macro`and- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await-macro`and- `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await-macro`and- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# half - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/half/^2/

## Expand description

A crate that provides support for half-precision 16-bit floating point types.

This crate provides the [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) type, which is an implementation of the IEEE 754-2008 standard

[a.k.a “half” floating point type. This 16-bit floating point type is intended for efficient storage where the full range and precision of a larger floating point value is not required. This is especially useful for image storage formats.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-precision_floating-point_format)

`binary16`This crate also provides a [ bf16](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html) type, an alternative 16-bit floating point format. The

[format is a truncated IEEE 754 standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bfloat16_floating-point_format)

`bfloat16``binary32` float that preserves the
exponent to allow the same range as [but with only 8 bits of precision (instead of 11 bits for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`[). See the](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html)

`f16`[type for details.](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`Because [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) and

[are primarily for efficient storage, floating point operations such as addition, multiplication, etc. are not always implemented by hardware. When hardware does not support these operations, this crate emulates them by converting the value to](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`[before performing the operation and then back afterward.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`Note that conversion from [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)/

[to both](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html)

`f16`[are lossy operations, and just as converting a](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`[to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

`f64`[is lossy and does not have](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32``Into`/`From` trait
implementations, so too do these smaller types not have those trait implementations either.
Instead, use `from_f32`/`from_f64` functions for the types in this crate. If you don’t care
about lossy conversions and need trait conversions, use the appropriate [traits that are implemented.](https://crates.io/crates/num-traits)

`num-traits`This crate also provides a [ slice](https://docs.rs/slice/index.html) module for zero-copy in-place conversions of

[slices to both](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u16.html)

`u16`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html)

`f16`[, as well as efficient vectorized conversions of larger buffers of floating point values to and from these half formats.](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`The crate supports `#[no_std]` when the `std` cargo feature is not enabled, so can be used in
embedded environments without using the Rust [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/) library. The

`std` feature enables support
for the standard library and is enabled by default, see the [Cargo Features](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)section below.

A [ prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html) module is provided for easy importing of available utility traits.

[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

When the `serde` feature is enabled, [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) and

[will be serialized as a newtype of](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16`[by default. In binary formats this is ideal, as it will generally use just two bytes for storage. For string formats like JSON, however, this isn’t as useful, and due to design limitations of serde, it’s not possible for the default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u16.html)

`u16``Serialize` implementation to support
different serialization for different formats.Instead, it’s up to the containter type of the floats to control how it is serialized. This can
easily be controlled when using the derive macros using `#[serde(serialize_with="")]`
attributes. For both [ f16](https://docs.rs/struct.f16.html) and

[a](https://docs.rs/struct.bf16.html)

`bf16``serialize_as_f32` and `serialize_as_string` are
provided for use with this attribute.Deserialization of both float types supports deserializing from the default serialization,
strings, and `f32`/`f64` values, so no additional work is required.

[§](https://docs.rs#hardware-support)Hardware support

Hardware support for these conversions and arithmetic will be used
whenever hardware support is available—either through instrinsics or targeted assembly—although
a nightly Rust toolchain may be required for some hardware. When hardware supports it the
functions and traits in the [ slice](https://docs.rs/slice/index.html) and

[modules will also use vectorized SIMD intructions for increased efficiency.](https://docs.rs/vec/index.html)

`vec`The following list details hardware support for floating point types in this crate. When using
`std` cargo feature, runtime CPU target detection will be used. To get the most performance
benefits, compile for specific CPU features which avoids the runtime overhead and works in a
`no_std` environment.

| Architecture | CPU Target Feature | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x86`/`x86_64` | `f16c` | This supports conversion to/from only (including vector SIMD) and does not support any`f16`or arithmetic operations.`bf16` |
| `aarch64` | `fp16` | This supports all operations on only.`f16` |
| `loongarch64` | `lsx` | This supports conversion to/from only (including vector SIMD) and does not support any`f16`or arithmetic operations.`bf16` |

# js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/js-sys/0.3.103/target-redirect/js_sys/

## Expand description

Bindings to JavaScript’s standard, built-in objects, including their methods and properties.

This does *not* include any Web, Node, or any other JS environment
APIs. Only the things that are guaranteed to exist in the global scope by
the ECMAScript standard.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-about-camelcase-snake_case-and-naming-conventions)A Note About `camelCase`, `snake_case`, and Naming Conventions

JavaScript’s global objects use `camelCase` naming conventions for functions
and methods, but Rust style is to use `snake_case`. These bindings expose
the Rust style `snake_case` name. Additionally, acronyms within a method
name are all lower case, where as in JavaScript they are all upper case. For
example, `decodeURI` in JavaScript is exposed as `decode_uri` in these
bindings.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-about-tostring-and-to_js_string)A Note About `toString` and `to_js_string`

JavaScript’s `toString()` method is exposed as `to_js_string()` in these
bindings to avoid confusion with Rust’s [ ToString](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html) trait and its

`to_string()` method. This allows types to implement both the Rust
[trait (which provides](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display``to_string()` via
[) and still expose the JavaScript](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/trait.ToString.html)

`ToString``toString()` functionality.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [wasm_bindgen](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [Atomics](https://docs.rs/Atomics/index.html)
- The `Atomics`object provides atomic operations as static methods. They are used with`SharedArrayBuffer`objects.
- [Intl](https://docs.rs/Intl/index.html)

- The `JSON`object contains methods for parsing[JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)](https://json.org/)and converting values to JSON. It can’t be called or constructed, and aside from its two method properties, it has no interesting functionality of its own.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_uri.html)- uri
- The `decodeURI()`function decodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) previously created by`encodeURI`or by a similar routine.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_uri_component.html)- uri_ - component
- The `decodeURIComponent()`function decodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) component previously created by`encodeURIComponent`or by a similar routine.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_uri.html)- uri
- The `encodeURI()`function encodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) by replacing each instance of certain characters by one, two, three, or four escape sequences representing the UTF-8 encoding of the character (will only be four escape sequences for characters composed of two “surrogate” characters).
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_uri_component.html)- uri_ - component
- The `encodeURIComponent()`function encodes a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) component by replacing each instance of certain characters by one, two, three, or four escape sequences representing the UTF-8 encoding of the character (will only be four escape sequences for characters composed of two “surrogate” characters).
- [escape](https://docs.rs/fn.escape.html)
- The `escape()`function computes a new string in which certain characters have been replaced by a hexadecimal escape sequence.
- [eval](https://docs.rs/fn.eval.html)
- The `eval()`function evaluates JavaScript code represented as a string.
- [global](https://docs.rs/fn.global.html)
- Returns a handle to the global scope object.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_finite.html)- finite
- The global `isFinite()`function determines whether the passed value is a finite number. If needed, the parameter is first converted to a number.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_float.html)- float
- The `parseFloat()`function parses an argument and returns a floating point number, or NaN on error.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_int.html)- int
- The `parseInt()`function parses a string argument and returns an integer of the specified radix (the base in mathematical numeral systems), or NaN on error.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_iter.html)- iter
- Create an iterator over `val`using the JS iteration protocol and`Symbol.iterator`.
- [unescape](https://docs.rs/fn.unescape.html)
- The `unescape()`function computes a new string in which hexadecimal escape sequences are replaced with the character that it represents. The escape sequences might be introduced by a function like`escape`. Usually,`decodeURI`or`decodeURIComponent`are preferred over`unescape`.

# AggregateError in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/=0.3.103/struct.AggregateError.html

`pub struct AggregateError { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `AggregateError` object represents an error when several errors need
to be wrapped in a single error. It is thrown when multiple errors need
to be reported by an operation, for example by [ Promise::any](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html#method.any), when
all promises passed to it reject.

`AggregateError` is a subclass of [ Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html).

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# Promise in js_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/js-sys/=0.3.103/struct.Promise.html

`pub struct Promise<T = `[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `Promise` with the provided executor `cb`

The `cb` is a function that is passed with the arguments `resolve` and
`reject`. The `cb` function is executed immediately by the `Promise`
implementation, passing `resolve` and `reject` functions (the executor
is called before the `Promise` constructor even returns the created
object). The `resolve` and `reject` functions, when called, resolve or
reject the promise, respectively. The executor normally initiates
some asynchronous work, and then, once that completes, either calls
the `resolve` function to resolve the promise or else rejects it if an
error occurred.

If an error is thrown in the executor function, the promise is rejected. The return value of the executor is ignored.

#### pub fn [all_iterable](https://docs.rs#method.all_iterable)<I>(

The `Promise.all(iterable)` method returns a single `Promise` that
resolves when all of the promises in the iterable argument have resolved
or when the iterable argument contains no promises. It rejects with the
reason of the first promise that rejects.

The `Promise.allSettled(iterable)` method returns a single `Promise` that
resolves when all of the promises in the iterable argument have either
fulfilled or rejected or when the iterable argument contains no promises.

The `Promise.any(iterable)` method returns a single `Promise` that
resolves when any of the promises in the iterable argument have resolved
or when the iterable argument contains no promises. It rejects with an
`AggregateError` if all promises in the iterable rejected.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13097)#### pub fn [any_iterable](https://docs.rs#method.any_iterable)<I>(obj: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<<I::[Item](https://docs.rs/trait.Iterable.html#associatedtype.Item) as [Promising](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html)>::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13097)

#### pub fn [any_iterable](https://docs.rs#method.any_iterable)<I>(obj: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<<I::[Item](https://docs.rs/trait.Iterable.html#associatedtype.Item) as [Promising](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html)>::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>

The `Promise.any(iterable)` method returns a single `Promise` that
resolves when any of the promises in the iterable argument have resolved
or when the iterable argument contains no promises. It rejects with an
`AggregateError` if all promises in the iterable rejected.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13097)#### pub fn [race_iterable](https://docs.rs#method.race_iterable)<I>(obj: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<<I::[Item](https://docs.rs/trait.Iterable.html#associatedtype.Item) as [Promising](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html)>::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13097)

#### pub fn [race_iterable](https://docs.rs#method.race_iterable)<I>(obj: [&I](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<<I::[Item](https://docs.rs/trait.Iterable.html#associatedtype.Item) as [Promising](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html)>::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>

The `Promise.race(iterable)` method returns a promise that resolves or
rejects as soon as one of the promises in the iterable resolves or
rejects, with the value or reason from that promise.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13097)#### pub fn [resolve](https://docs.rs#method.resolve)<U>(obj: [&U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<U::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13097)

#### pub fn [resolve](https://docs.rs#method.resolve)<U>(obj: [&U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<U::[Resolution](https://docs.rs/trait.Promising.html#associatedtype.Resolution)>

The `Promise.resolve(value)` method returns a `Promise` object that is
resolved with the given value. If the value is a promise, that promise
is returned; if the value is a thenable (i.e. has a “then” method), the
returned promise will “follow” that thenable, adopting its eventual
state; otherwise the returned promise will be fulfilled with the value.

The `catch()` method returns a `Promise` and deals with rejected cases
only.  It behaves the same as calling `Promise.prototype.then(undefined, onRejected)` (in fact, calling `obj.catch(onRejected)` internally calls
`obj.then(undefined, onRejected)`).

[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)>>,

The `finally()` method returns a `Promise`. When the promise is settled,
whether fulfilled or rejected, the specified callback function is
executed. This provides a way for code that must be executed once the
`Promise` has been dealt with to be run whether the promise was
fulfilled successfully or rejected.

This lets you avoid duplicating code in both the promise’s `then()` and
`catch()` handlers.

Heterogeneous counterpart to [ Promise::all_iterable](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html#method.all_iterable): accepts a Rust
tuple of

`Promise<T_i>` and returns a single [resolving to a typed](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)

`Promise`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrayTuple.html)

`ArrayTuple<(T_1, T_2, ..., T_n)>`Destructure the awaited result via [ ArrayTuple::into_tuple](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrayTuple.html#method.into_tuple) to get
the individual values back as a native Rust tuple. Implemented for
arity 1..=8.

Rejects with the first rejection, matching `Promise.all` semantics.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#13566-13568)

#### pub fn [all_settled_tuple](https://docs.rs#method.all_settled_tuple)<T: PromiseTuple>(promises: T) -> [Promise](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)<T::Settled>

Heterogeneous counterpart to [ Promise::all_settled_iterable](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html#method.all_settled_iterable): accepts
a Rust tuple of

`Promise<T_i>` and returns a single [resolving to a typed](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html)

`Promise``ArrayTuple<(PromiseState<T_1>, ..., PromiseState<T_n>)>`.Unlike [ Promise::all_tuple](https://docs.rs/struct.Promise.html#method.all_tuple), this never rejects early: every input
settles (fulfills or rejects) and is reflected by its

[slot in the result tuple. Implemented for arity 1..=8.](https://docs.rs/struct.PromiseState.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

The `Array.fromAsync()` static method with a map function creates a new, shallow-copied
`Array` instance from an async iterable, iterable or array-like object, applying the map
function to each value.

The `findIndex()` method returns the index of the first element in the array that
satisfies the provided testing function. Otherwise -1 is returned.

**Note:** Consider using [ Array::try_find_index](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html#method.try_find_index) if the predicate might throw an error.

The `findLast()` method of Array instances iterates the array in reverse order
and returns the value of the first element that satisfies the provided testing function.
If no elements satisfy the testing function, undefined is returned.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

If no elements satisfy the testing function, undefined is returned. *(Fallible variation)*

The `findLastIndex()` method of Array instances iterates the array in reverse order
and returns the index of the first element that satisfies the provided testing function.
If no elements satisfy the testing function, -1 is returned.

**Note:** Consider using [ Array::try_find_last_index](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html#method.try_find_last_index) if the predicate might throw an error.

The `lastIndexOf()` method returns the last index at which a given element
can be found in the array, or -1 if it is not present. The array is
searched backwards, starting at fromIndex.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)#### pub fn [set_length](https://docs.rs#method.set_length)(&self, value: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

#### pub fn [set_length](https://docs.rs#method.set_length)(&self, value: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html))

Sets the length of the array.

If it is set to less than the current length of the array, it will shrink the array.

If it is set to more than the current length of the array, it will increase the length of the array, filling the new space with empty slots.

`map()` calls a provided callback function once for each element in an array,
in order, and constructs a new array from the results. callback is invoked
only for indexes of the array which have assigned values, including undefined.
It is not called for missing elements of the array (that is, indexes that have
never been set, which have been deleted or which have never been assigned a value).

**Note:** Consider using [ Array::try_map](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html#method.try_map) for safer fallible handling.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

`map()` calls a provided callback function once for each element in an array,
in order, and constructs a new array from the results. callback is invoked
only for indexes of the array which have assigned values, including undefined.
It is not called for missing elements of the array (that is, indexes that have
never been set, which have been deleted or which have never been assigned a value).
*(Fallible variation)*

The `Array.of()` method creates a new Array instance with a variable
number of arguments, regardless of number or type of the arguments.

Note: For type inference use `Array::<T>::of(&[T])`.

The difference between `Array.of()` and the `Array` constructor is in the
handling of integer arguments: `Array.of(7)` creates an array with a single
element, `7`, whereas `Array(7)` creates an empty array with a `length`
property of `7` (Note: this implies an array of 7 empty slots, not slots
with actual undefined values).

The `shift()` method removes the first element from an array and returns
that removed element. This method changes the length of the array.

**Note:** Consider using [ Array::shift_checked](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html#method.shift_checked) for handling empty arrays.

The `some()` method tests whether at least one element in the array passes the test implemented
by the provided function.
Note: This method returns false for any condition put on an empty array.

**Note:** Consider using [ Array::try_some](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html#method.try_some) if the predicate might throw an error.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

The `some()` method tests whether at least one element in the array passes the test implemented
by the provided function. *(Fallible variation)*
Note: This method returns false for any condition put on an empty array.
[MDN documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/some)

The `sort()` method sorts the elements of an array in place and returns
the array. The sort is not necessarily stable. The default sort
order is according to string Unicode code points.

The time and space complexity of the sort cannot be guaranteed as it is implementation dependent.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#526)

#### pub fn [to_locale_string](https://docs.rs#method.to_locale_string)(&self, locales: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html), options: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [JsString](https://docs.rs/struct.JsString.html)

The `toLocaleString()` method returns a string representing the elements of the array.
The elements are converted to Strings using their toLocaleString methods and these
Strings are separated by a locale-specific String (such as a comma “,”).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#2097-2105)#### pub fn [from_iter_typed](https://docs.rs#method.from_iter_typed)<A, I>(iter: I) -> [Array](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#2097-2105)

#### pub fn [from_iter_typed](https://docs.rs#method.from_iter_typed)<A, I>(iter: I) -> [Array](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html)<T>

Collect an iterator into a typed `Array<T>`, projecting each item
through its canonical [ JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html) via

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html)

`IntoJsGeneric`This is the typed counterpart to the stable
`impl FromIterator<A> for Array where A: AsRef<JsValue>`, which always
produces an erased `Array<JsValue>`. Use `from_iter_typed` when you
want the element type inferred from the iterator item:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use js_sys::{Array, Number};
let arr = Array::from_iter_typed((0..10).map(Number::from));
// arr: Array<Number>
```
Reference iteration (`Item = &U`) is supported transparently via the
`&U: IntoJsGeneric` blanket in `wasm-bindgen` core.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#6861)#### pub fn [has_own_property](https://docs.rs#method.has_own_property)(&self, property: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Use `Object::hasOwn` instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#6861)

#### pub fn [has_own_property](https://docs.rs#method.has_own_property)(&self, property: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Use `Object::hasOwn` instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

`Some(slice)`. The returned
`WasmSlice` is either a borrow of the input slice (primitive
case) or a buffer JS owns and frees (handle-shaped case).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#2170)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(length: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [ArrayBuffer](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrayBuffer.html)

The `ArrayBuffer` object is used to represent a generic,
fixed-length raw binary data buffer. You cannot directly
manipulate the contents of an `ArrayBuffer`; instead, you
create one of the typed array objects or a `DataView` object
which represents the buffer in a specific format, and use that
to read and write the contents of the buffer.

fixed-length raw binary data buffer. You cannot directly
manipulate the contents of an `ArrayBuffer`; instead, you
create one of the typed array objects or a `DataView` object
which represents the buffer in a specific format, and use that
to read and write the contents of the buffer.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#2170)

#### pub fn [byte_length](https://docs.rs#method.byte_length)(&self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

The `byteLength` property of an object which is an instance of type ArrayBuffer
it’s an accessor property whose set accessor function is undefined,
meaning that you can only read this property.
The value is established when the array is constructed and cannot be changed.
This property returns 0 if this ArrayBuffer has been detached.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

#### pub fn [has_own_property](https://docs.rs#method.has_own_property)(&self, property: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Use `Object::hasOwn` instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

#### type [Anchor](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/traits/trait.RefFromWasmAbi.html#associatedtype.Anchor) = [ManuallyDrop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/manually_drop/struct.ManuallyDrop.html)<[ArrayTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrayTuple.html)<T>>

`Self` for the duration of the
invocation of the function that has an `&Self` parameter. This is
required to ensure that the lifetimes don’t persist beyond one function
call, and so that they remain anonymous.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#1823)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

### impl<T> [AsyncIterator](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncIterator.html)<T>

The `next()` method always has to return a Promise which resolves to an object
with appropriate properties including done and value. If a non-object value
gets returned (such as false or undefined), a TypeError (“iterator.next()
returned a non-object value”) will be thrown.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

#### pub unsafe fn [view](https://docs.rs#method.view)(rust: &[[i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html)]) -> [BigInt64Array](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt64Array.html)

Creates a JS typed array which is a view into wasm’s linear memory at the slice specified.

This function returns a new typed array which is a view into wasm’s memory. This view does not copy the underlying data.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Views into WebAssembly memory are only valid so long as the
backing buffer isn’t resized in JS. Once this function is called
any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated but the input slice isn’t guaranteed to be mutable.

Finally, the returned object is disconnected from the input slice’s lifetime, so there’s no guarantee that the data is read at the right time.

any future calls to `Box::new` (or malloc of any form) may cause
the returned value here to be invalidated. Use with caution!

Additionally the returned object can be safely mutated, the changes are guaranteed to be reflected in the input array.

#### pub fn [has_own_property](https://docs.rs#method.has_own_property)(&self, property: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Use `Object::hasOwn` instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#14136-14180)

#### pub fn [copy_to_uninit](https://docs.rs#method.copy_to_uninit)<'dst>(
    &self,
    dst: &'dst mut [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>],
) -> &'dst mut [[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)]

Copy the contents of this JS typed array into the destination Rust slice.

This function will efficiently copy the memory from a typed array into this Wasm module’s own linear memory, initializing the memory destination provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

This function will panic if this typed array’s length is
different than the length of the provided `dst` array.

Copy the contents of the source Rust slice into this JS typed array.

This function will efficiently copy the memory from within the Wasm module’s own linear memory to this typed array.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

This function will panic if this typed array’s length is
different than the length of the provided `src` array.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#6861)#### pub fn [has_own_property](https://docs.rs#method.has_own_property)(&self, property: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Use `Object::hasOwn` instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/js_sys/lib.rs.html#6861)

#### pub fn [has_own_property](https://docs.rs#method.has_own_property)(&self, property: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Use `Object::hasOwn` instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#191)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#194)

[Source](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#197)

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

#### fn [slice_into_abi](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/slices/trait.VectorRefIntoWasmAbi.html#tymethod.slice_into_abi)(slice: &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)) -> [WasmSlice](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/convert/slices/struct.WasmSlice.html)

`Some(slice)`. The returned
`WasmSlice` is either a borrow of the input slice (primitive
case) or a buffer JS owns and frees (handle-shaped case).
